statements.text: Classroom projects can cause some conflicts in a group.
It's bad when people don't do their share for a project.
Teachers enjoy classroom projects more than students.
Classroom projects can be inconvenient for students.
Classroom projects should not be the same all the time.

audio_transcript.speaker: A
audio_transcript.text: As for me, I like it when our teachers ask us to do some project. In my opinion, projects allow students to work together to show what they have learned. We work on too many solo activities throughout the day, and giving us a chance to collaborate is a nice change. Working together helps us to complete more work in a shorter amount of time. Plus, if we are confused about a concept, it is likely that our classmates will help explain concepts to us.

audio_transcript.speaker: B
audio_transcript.text: Well, classroom projects are certainly more interesting than traditional paper-and-pencil tests, but I think they still do not reach every learning style or intelligence level. Our teachers always ask us to make presentations as classroom projects. I'm an introvert, and I find frequent presentations hard. My grades suffer because of them. If our teachers plan a variety of projects, or even let students choose what kind of project they'll do, it will be much better.

audio_transcript.speaker: C
audio_transcript.text: I hate classroom projects. Honestly, we've all been there. It's 11:50 p.m. and your project is due at midnight. And there's one person who hasn't done their part yet, so you quickly scramble to do it yourself. Or when you have a presentation, and you have no idea whether or not people in your group actually know what they are presenting on. It's so annoying. I prefer to do everything on my own, as I don't like it when I depend on other people in terms of my grades.

audio_transcript.speaker: D
audio_transcript.text: Our teachers always tell us that a classroom project is a perfect chance for us to learn how to collaborate with one another. However, I disagree with them here. Even if you know your group members well enough, some of them may not be able to work well together, especially if there are two people in a group who both want to be the leader. Compromise is certainly the key to getting through group projects, but it's just not always possible, in my opinion.

audio_transcript.speaker: E
audio_transcript.text: I think it's worth doing projects, but there can be a huge problem connected with doing a project in a group. Sometimes students are put together in groups by their professors, but these students can have conflicting schedules. Every college student has a different schedule. There are extracurricular activities and even part-time jobs that we have, too. I wish professors would take this into consideration when picking our groups for us and assigning group projects.

audio_transcript.speaker: F
audio_transcript.text: As for me, I enjoy doing projects at school. First of all, I think students have more control over their education with project-based learning. They have to make choices and be responsible for their academic performance. Secondly, classroom projects enable students to understand the material much better. Thirdly, it's a great chance to improve your communication skills, as you have to collaborate with your groupmates to complete a classroom project.

statements.text: Ben worked hard during the academic year.
Ben and Sophie study at the same school.
Sophie wants to be a school teacher.
Sophie has already found a summer job.
Ben is thinking of a career in medicine.
Ben disapproves of Sophie's summer plans.
Sophie hasn't had a rest by the sea for some time.

audio_transcript.speaker: Ben
audio_transcript.text: Hey, Sophie! Long time, no see! How are you?

audio_transcript.speaker: Sophie
audio_transcript.text: Oh, hi, Ben. It's good to see you. I'm fine, thank you. What about you?

audio_transcript.speaker: Ben
audio_transcript.text: Oh, I'm fine too, thanks. So, it's summer vacation at last! I'm so happy all the tests and projects are over, at least for a couple of months. What are your plans?

audio_transcript.speaker: Sophie
audio_transcript.text: Oh, I'm so excited. I'm planning to look for a summer job, maybe as a camp counsellor. As you know, I love working with kids, and it seems like a fun way to spend the summer.

audio_transcript.speaker: Ben
audio_transcript.text: That's awesome! I thought about that too, but I decided to volunteer at the hospital instead. I want to see what it's like behind the scenes.

audio_transcript.speaker: Sophie
audio_transcript.text: Wow, that's really impressive. Isn't it hard to get a volunteer spot there?

audio_transcript.speaker: Ben
audio_transcript.text: A bit, but I applied early. I want to see what it's like to work in healthcare, and maybe get some experience for the future.

audio_transcript.speaker: Sophie
audio_transcript.text: That's smart. I want to gain some experience working with kids, so camp counselling seems perfect for me. It's also a good way to meet new people.

audio_transcript.speaker: Ben
audio_transcript.text: Have you applied yet?

audio_transcript.speaker: Sophie
audio_transcript.text: Not yet. I'm going to a job fair tomorrow to see what's available. Hopefully, I'll find something interesting. Summer is the busiest time for camps for kids. I do hope they'll be interested in me.

audio_transcript.speaker: Ben
audio_transcript.text: Good luck! I hope you'll find something you like. I believe it's important to enjoy what you do.

audio_transcript.speaker: Sophie
audio_transcript.text: Thanks! What made you want to volunteer at the hospital? It must be very hard to work there. It's not like you'll be able to breathe some fresh air at this job.

audio_transcript.speaker: Ben
audio_transcript.text: I'm thinking about studying medicine in the future, so I want to see if it's really for me. Plus, I want to help people. It's great to give back to the community, right?

audio_transcript.speaker: Sophie
audio_transcript.text: That's a great idea. I wish I knew what I wanted to do later. Sometimes it feels overwhelming.

audio_transcript.speaker: Ben
audio_transcript.text: Don't worry, you have plenty of time. Besides, working with kids is super important too. You'll be able to gain some valuable skills.

audio_transcript.speaker: Sophie
audio_transcript.text: True! Maybe we could both try volunteering at each other's places one day. It would be interesting to do.

audio_transcript.speaker: Ben
audio_transcript.text: That would be fun! I'd love to see what camp counselling is like. Maybe I could learn some new things.

audio_transcript.speaker: Sophie
audio_transcript.text: And I'm curious about the hospital. Maybe we can arrange a visit sometime.

audio_transcript.speaker: Ben
audio_transcript.text: For sure! By the way, do you fancy going to the beach this weekend? It's supposed to be really sunny, and it would be a nice break.

audio_transcript.speaker: Sophie
audio_transcript.text: I'd love to! Let's do it. It's been a while since I relaxed by the sea. We can get some food and organize a picnic.

audio_transcript.speaker: Ben
audio_transcript.text: I think I'll get a ball too.

audio_transcript.speaker: Sophie
audio_transcript.text: It's a date then.

shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.speaker: Presenter
shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.text: Hello, everybody, and here we are with our weekly programme, Five Minutes with a Star. Today in our studio we are happy to have Mike Watson, the famous comedy actor and film director, as well as the winner of numerous awards. Good afternoon, Mike!

shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.speaker: Mike Watson
shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.text: Good afternoon. Thank you for inviting me here today.

shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.speaker: Presenter
shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.text: As an actor and a film director, are you upset when you see a bad movie?

shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.speaker: Mike Watson
shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.text: In my opinion, films have unparalleled power to influence culture. Of course, it bothers me to see that power abused. It appalls me when that power is abused to make money, to show irresponsible acts or even violence, and essentially give people a Roman circus in a movie theater for 10 dollars. I get upset after seeing some films. Some of them are completely awful.

shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.speaker: Presenter
shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.text: Do you see your job as kind of a responsibility then?

shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.speaker: Mike Watson
shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.text: No, I mean anybody can do anything they want. But the power of films to move, the power to serve as a mirror for our society, the power to spread a sense of humanity and make people laugh – never stop to impress me. Chaplin made the whole world laugh for the very first time at the same things, and with no words. Film is truly a universal language. Like so many things, I wish it were used more as a weapon of beauty, rather than a weapon of ugliness.

shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.speaker: Presenter
shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.text: Have you always wanted to be a film director?

shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.speaker: Mike Watson
shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.text: I've been a genuine film fan for about as long as I can remember. I've always been crazy about movies. And then I went to Stanford and was considering which graduate school to apply to. And I wasn't even thinking that I wanted to be a film director, I was thinking that I wanted to go to a film school. I just wanted to see what that was, and see if my love of watching films would translate into loving making them.

shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.speaker: Mike Watson
shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.text: It did. And I had the patience for it. One does not know the dedication it requires and how time-consuming it is to make a movie until you do it. And I liked it. I was certainly not the most talented student in my group, but I still found I had just enough talent to be able to build on.

shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.speaker: Presenter
shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.text: Do you think that your academic education is beneficial to you now as a director?

shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.speaker: Mike Watson
shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.text: I do have to credit my education in literature and history. You study the human story of what people do, and try to get at why they do those things, – a sense of narrative. History is narrative; and literature is obviously narrative – presenting characters, selecting events from their lives, and getting at motivations. The best historians write with the same urgency and flourish as great novelists. The great historians have a prose style as fluid and compelling as novelists do.

shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.speaker: Presenter
shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.text: You were 35 when you made your first feature film. Does it necessarily take a long time to become a director?

shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.speaker: Mike Watson
shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.text: Not for everybody, but for me it did. I was 35, but that's a fairly standard average age for making a first feature film. Many high-profile film directors made their first feature film at about that age, like mid-thirties, and don't forget that back then, everybody started working earlier, too.

shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.speaker: Presenter
shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.text: Don't you think that's for a good reason? I mean, it's hard for a 25-year-old person to handle a 20-million-dollar budget.

shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.speaker: Mike Watson
shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.text: You don't need 20 million dollars to make a feature film nowadays. We live in an age where there are no more excuses. The means of production are readily accessible. You can make a feature film with your smartphone. It's amazing – the age we live in. You have a movie camera in your pocket, and it's even with sync-sound. It's unbelievable. When something is happening, you can just point your phone camera at it.

shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.speaker: Presenter
shared_audio_transcript_for_tasks_3_9.text: Thank you very much, Mike. It was nice talking to you.

texts.text: The magnificent lion is the symbol of Africa. Powerful and beautiful, the king of the beasts has no natural enemies. Lions have strong, compact bodies and powerful forelegs, teeth, and jaws for pulling down their food. Their coats are yellow-gold, and adult males have manes that range in colour from blond, to reddish-brown and black. The length and the colour of a lion's mane are likely determined by age, genetics, and hormones. Young lions have light spots on their coats that disappear as they grow.

Lions are mammals and the most sociable of all big cats. They live in groups called prides, which usually consist of related females and their cubs. Males often fight to maintain dominance. Young females usually stay in their mothers' prides for life, unless food shortage forces them out. Young males are driven from their prides when they grow large enough to compete with the dominant males. This usually happens when young males are between the ages of 2 and 4.

Today, lions are not at risk of extinction in Africa. However, three-quarters of their populations are in decline. The main threats to African lions are conflicts with people and the loss of living space, as well as climate change and wildlife trade. Some African lion populations have become small and isolated. Besides, the number of plant-eating animals they hunt for is being reduced. With around 23,000 African lions left in the wild, they are now officially classified as "vulnerable".

African lions are highly adaptable animals and can be found in a wide variety of habitats, including desert areas. They prefer open woodland and thick bush, as well as scrub and grasslands. Such environments help them to hunt and also to find shade to rest during the hottest part of the day. African lions used to be spread across most of the continent. But now they are only found in sub-Saharan Africa, with 80 % in eastern or southern Africa. Three of the five largest populations are in Tanzania.

Lions are top hunters in their environments, whether that is grassland, desert, or open woodland. It means they play an important role in keeping a healthy balance of numbers among other animals, especially plant-eating ones, like zebra and wildebeest. This influences the condition of grasslands and forests. By protecting a lion's landscape, people are helping the whole area to grow and develop, which does not just benefit wildlife, but the people who rely on local natural resources, too.

Lions do most of their hunting at night as their eyes have adapted to the dark. This gives them a huge advantage over the animals they hunt for. Interestingly, lions also hunt during storms. The noise, rain, and wind make it harder for other animals to see and hear lions, increasing their chances of a successful hunt. Females are the primary hunters, although males will sometimes join them during a hunt. When hunting, females have specific roles. Some chase the animal towards those in the centre.

To save lions, new protected areas of habitat in east Africa are organised. There is a special conservation programme in Kenya that monitors and protects lions. The programme educates local people on lion conservation, too. This includes working with local communities, such as anti-poisoning actions. They also provide better fenced areas for farm animals in local villages. Taking school children on trips to see the wild animals they are saving is one more important action to support wildlife.

tasks.shared_text:
No matter what your occupation is, you have probably faced some uncertainty over the last few years as a result of innovative Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology and its growing popularity. Teachers and students alike feel strongly about the upcoming changes. There are certain ways in which AI technology is altering education, both for teachers and students. Here is what lies ahead for education and the student experience in today's AI-driven world.
If you have tried using AI tools yourself, you know how powerful they can be. With just a few clicks, these programmes can write stories, organise ideas, and even complete homework assignments. Unfortunately for educators, this potent tool is also available to students who may use it to cheat and plagiarise work. Over the last several months, teachers from elementary schools to universities have been trying to address this growing problem.
Sadly, there is, as yet, no silver-bullet solution for teachers. While some software has claimed to be able to detect the presence of AI-generated content, none of these have fully cracked the code. Teachers are now left to guess whether students are using this software to complete assignments. As a result of this change, there will likely be a shift in education that puts emphasis on in-person assessments, rather than take-home assignments. In this way, educators can be sure that students are not using AI software to generate their work.
But AI is not just causing problems – it is also creating new opportunities. Teachers are also starting to introduce AI into their processes. Instead of banning the use of AI, many educators and institutions are currently trying to figure out the best ways for students to use this technology as a helpful tool. Some teachers believe that soon, all students will learn how to use AI properly to support their learning in honest and useful ways.
Over the decades, a critique of the school system has been its one-size-fits-all approach to education. This is a model that treats every student the same way, ignoring individual needs and learning styles. Though there were some attempts to fix this issue, none have been very effective. Today, however, AI is presenting itself as an antidote to this problem. The data about students' abilities makes it possible for teachers to use AI to personalise learning. For example, the technology can show which students need extra help, and which ones are ready for more challenging work. This means teachers can tweak their lessons to fit each student's needs, helping everyone do their best.
Getting extra help outside of school has always been important for many students, but not everyone could afford private tutors. Now, AI is changing that. Free AI tutors are becoming available to help students with their schoolwork anytime they need it. These digital tutors can explain difficult concepts, help with homework, and give students the extra practice they need to understand tough subjects.
Thus, AI can have a wide variety of impacts on the student experience. While it is creating new problems, like cheating, it is also offering new ways to make learning more personal and accessible for every student. Now, all students have more opportunities to excel in subjects they once found challenging. This incredible innovation makes me hopeful that more students will achieve academic success. The key will be learning how to use this technology wisely – as a tool to support learning, not replace it. As teachers and students continue to adapt, one thing is clear: education will never again be the same.

counting_rules: Contracted forms (can't, didn't, isn't, I'm, etc.) count as one word.
Numerals written as digits (1, 25, 2009, 126 204) count as one word.
Numerals with % sign (25%, 100%) count as one word.
Numerals written as words count as words (each word counted).
Compound words (good-looking, well-bred, English-speaking, twenty-five) count as one word.
Abbreviations (USA, e-mail, TV, CD-rom) count as one word.
Salutation and signature in an email are counted.
